outcomes: Express parameter estimation as a model, scalar loss, gradient computation, and update rule.
Explain what autograd records and why gradients accumulate on leaf tensors.
Write a correct optimizer loop and a gradient-free validation loop.
Diagnose unstable learning by inspecting scale, learning rate, loss history, and finite gradients.

sections.title: Begin with a model you can inspect
sections.summary: A two-parameter temperature conversion exposes every moving part of learning.
body: The chapter's temperature example predicts a known target from an observed measurement using a scale parameter and a bias. The values start wrong, but the model is differentiable: a small change in either parameter produces a measurable change in the prediction and loss.

A simple model is not a toy to skip. It lets us verify the loss surface, gradient sign, update direction, and unit scale before neural-network layers hide those details behind thousands of parameters.

code.title: Model and mean-squared error

points: The model maps observations to predictions.
The loss reduces all prediction errors to one optimization objective.
Parameters are the values the update rule is allowed to change.
The dataset and objective define what a good parameter means.

sections.title: See how scale controls optimization
sections.summary: A mathematically valid gradient can still produce an unusable update when features or the learning rate are poorly scaled.
body: The derivative with respect to a parameter includes the magnitude of its input. If temperature observations are tens of units while the bias input is effectively one, the scale gradient can be much larger than the bias gradient. A shared learning rate may then overshoot.

Normalize inputs using statistics fitted on training data or choose parameter-specific optimization deliberately. Always inspect finite loss and gradient values when training diverges; reducing the learning rate without understanding scale can hide the root cause.

code.title: Normalize one feature
code.source:
import torch

train_observed = torch.tensor([35.7, 58.2, 81.9, 56.3, 33.9, 21.8, 60.4, 68.4])
train_mean = train_observed.mean()
train_std = train_observed.std().clamp_min(1e-8)
train_observed_normalized = (train_observed - train_mean) / train_std

assert abs(train_observed_normalized.mean().item()) < 1e-6
assert torch.isfinite(train_observed_normalized).all().item()

callouts.title: Fit statistics before evaluation
callouts.body: Use only the training split to compute mean and standard deviation. Evaluation data must not influence the learned representation.

sections.title: Let autograd apply the chain rule
sections.summary: Operations involving requires-grad inputs build a graph that backward traverses from loss to leaves.
body: Autograd records operations during the forward pass when at least one required input participates. The resulting tensors point to gradient functions, while user-created parameters are normally leaves. Calling backward() on a scalar loss propagates derivatives through the graph and accumulates them in the .grad fields of eligible leaves.
The graph is rebuilt on each ordinary forward pass, which is why Python control flow can change between iterations. Do not detach an intermediate that the loss must differentiate through.

code.title: Inspect leaf gradients
code.source:
import torch

train_observed = torch.tensor([35.7, 58.2, 81.9, 56.3, 33.9, 21.8, 60.4, 68.4])
train_target = torch.tensor([0.5, 15.0, 28.0, 11.0, 3.0, -4.0, 13.0, 21.0])
train_observed_normalized = (train_observed - train_observed.mean()) / train_observed.std().clamp_min(1e-8)

def model(x, scale, bias):
    return scale * x + bias

def loss_fn(prediction, truth):
    return (prediction - truth).square().mean()

parameters = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0], requires_grad=True)
prediction = model(train_observed_normalized, parameters[0], parameters[1])
loss = loss_fn(prediction, train_target)
loss.backward()

print("loss grad_fn:", loss.grad_fn)
print("parameter grad:", parameters.grad)
assert parameters.is_leaf

callouts.title: Backward accumulates
callouts.body: After a new forward pass, calling backward without clearing adds to an existing leaf gradient. Calling backward twice on the same graph requires retain_graph=True and is normally unnecessary; ordinary optimizer steps should clear previous gradients first.

sections.title: Use the canonical optimizer sequence
sections.summary: Clear, predict, measure, differentiate, and step in a stable visible order.
body: An optimizer owns references to the parameters and applies an update rule using their gradients. It does not compute the loss or call backward. Keeping those responsibilities visible makes the loop easy to debug and generalizes to neural networks.

Optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) clears old gradients by setting their fields to None. This is the current default and can avoid unnecessary writes. It also makes a parameter that received no gradient distinguishable from one whose gradient is numerically zero.

code.title: A complete optimizer loop
code.source:
import torch

train_observed = torch.tensor([35.7, 58.2, 81.9, 56.3, 33.9, 21.8, 60.4, 68.4])
train_target = torch.tensor([0.5, 15.0, 28.0, 11.0, 3.0, -4.0, 13.0, 21.0])
validation_observed = torch.tensor([55.9, 48.9, 48.4])
validation_target = torch.tensor([14.0, 8.0, 6.0])

train_mean = train_observed.mean()
train_std = train_observed.std().clamp_min(1e-8)
train_observed_normalized = (train_observed - train_mean) / train_std

def model(x, scale, bias):
    return scale * x + bias

def loss_fn(prediction, truth):
    return (prediction - truth).square().mean()

parameters = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0], requires_grad=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([parameters], lr=0.05)

for step in range(500):
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    prediction = model(train_observed_normalized, parameters[0], parameters[1])
    loss = loss_fn(prediction, train_target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

assert torch.isfinite(parameters).all().item()
print(parameters.detach(), loss.item())

callouts.title: Do not update through .data
callouts.body: Use an optimizer or a no-grad block for deliberate manual updates. .data can mutate values without autograd's normal correctness checks.

sections.title: Measure generalization on a separate path
sections.summary: Validation uses fixed parameters and no optimizer, so gradient recording is unnecessary.
body: A falling training loss proves only that the optimizer fits the examples it sees. Hold out validation samples before fitting preprocessing statistics, then report validation loss at a useful interval. The validation path must not call backward or optimizer.step.
For modules, pair model.eval() with torch.inference_mode(). The temperature function has no train/eval state, but inference mode still communicates that the result will not participate in learning.

code.title: Gradient-free validation
code.source:
import torch

# Prerequisite: run "A complete optimizer loop" immediately above.
# It defines validation data, train-only statistics, model, loss_fn, and parameters.
validation_observed_normalized = (validation_observed - train_mean) / train_std

with torch.inference_mode():
    validation_prediction = model(
        validation_observed_normalized,
        parameters[0],
        parameters[1],
    )
    validation_loss = loss_fn(validation_prediction, validation_target)

print(validation_loss.item())

points: Never select a final result from test data repeatedly.
Record both training and validation curves.
Copy or serialize the best state rather than retaining a mutable reference.

sections.title: Debug learning with evidence
sections.summary: Loss curves, finite checks, gradient norms, and a tiny overfit test reveal different failure classes.
body: A flat loss can mean disconnected parameters, an excessively small learning rate, saturated operations, or constant inputs. An exploding or NaN loss can point to scale, division, invalid logarithms, or an excessive learning rate. Print representative gradients instead of guessing.

A powerful pipeline test is to overfit a tiny batch. If a model with enough capacity cannot drive that small training loss down, investigate data-target pairing, the forward path, loss assumptions, gradient presence, and update execution before running a long experiment.

code.title: Fail fast on invalid training state
code.source:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
y = torch.tensor([-2.0, 1.0, 4.0])
parameters = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0], requires_grad=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([parameters], lr=0.05)

for step in range(100):
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    prediction = parameters[0] * x + parameters[1]
    loss = (prediction - y).square().mean()
    if not torch.isfinite(loss).item():
        raise RuntimeError(f"non-finite loss at step {step}: {loss.item()}")

    loss.backward()
    if parameters.grad is None:
        raise RuntimeError("parameters received no gradient")
    if not torch.isfinite(parameters.grad).all().item():
        raise RuntimeError(f"non-finite gradient at step {step}")

    optimizer.step()
    if not torch.isfinite(parameters).all().item():
        raise RuntimeError(f"non-finite parameters after step {step}")

print(parameters.detach())

modern.book: The optimizer notebooks call zero_grad() before each backward pass.
modern.reason: Setting gradients to None is the current default, reduces memory writes, and distinguishes a missing gradient from a computed zero gradient.

modern.book: Small validation computations may run as ordinary tensor expressions.
modern.current: Use inference_mode() for validation and eval() when modules have training-dependent behavior
modern.reason: The explicit evaluation path avoids recording an unnecessary backward graph and prevents dropout or batch normalization from behaving as if training.

modern.book: The chapter focuses on transparent float32 optimization.
modern.current: Keep float32 as the teaching baseline and introduce torch.amp only as a measured extension
modern.reason: Autocast and gradient scaling can accelerate supported hardware, but they should follow a correct, numerically checked baseline.

exercises.title: Compare three gradient paths
exercises.prompt: Compute the scale and bias gradients by finite differences, by an analytic expression, and by autograd at the same parameter values. Report absolute differences.
exercises.success: all three methods agree within a stated tolerance and the finite-difference epsilon is justified

exercises.title: Expose gradient accumulation
exercises.prompt: Compute a forward pass and call backward, then recompute the same forward and loss and call backward again without clearing gradients. Record .grad after each call, then repeat with zero_grad(set_to_none=True). Explain why reusing the exact same graph would instead require retain_graph=True.
exercises.success: the uncleared gradient doubles after the recomputed identical calculation, the cleared path starts from None, and graph reuse is distinguished from gradient accumulation

exercises.title: Build a reviewed training loop
exercises.prompt: Train on one split, validate under inference_mode(), record both losses, reject non-finite values, and save a copy of the best parameters.
exercises.success: the best saved parameters reproduce the lowest recorded validation loss without any validation update
